articles.title: Moscow’s Afghan outreach
articles.content: RUSSIA’S growing engagement with Afghanistan’s Taliban rulers is reshaping the regional diplomatic landscape. For Pakistan, which has historically maintained close links with Afghan political and religious networks, the development presents both a challenge and an opportunity. The question is not whether Moscow will replace Islamabad as Kabul’s principal interlocutor, but whether Russia’s expanding diplomatic, security and economic engagement will give the Taliban greater room to manoeuvre in their dealings with Pakistan. Russia’s approach towards the Taliban has been gradually shaping up. In July 2025, Moscow became thefirst country to recognise the Taliban governmentformally. Earlier, it announced the removal of the Taliban from its list of prohibited terrorist organisations in April that year. In May 2026, Russian officials announced plans to establish a “full-fledged partnership” with Kabul, encompassing security, trade, cultural exchanges, and humanitarian cooperation. That same month, a military-technical cooperation arrangement further underscored the deepening relationship. Moscow, therefore, has been moving beyond limited diplomatic engagement towards a more sustained relationship with the Taliban authorities. Multiple factors may be shaping Moscow’s approach toward the Taliban. First, Moscow remains concerned about the spread of militant violence into Central Asia, narcotics trafficking, and the activities of Islamic State-Khorasan (IS-K). The deadly2024 attacknear Moscow reinforced Russian concerns about transnational extremist networks. From the Kremlin’s perspective, dealing with the Taliban is a pragmatic necessity — whatever its reservations about the nature of their government, the Taliban exercise effective control over Afghanistan’s state institutions and security apparatus. In parallel, Russia seeks to preserve its influence in Eurasia and prevent Afghanistan from becoming a source of instability that could invite renewed intervention by external powers. Economic cooperation, including potential opportunities in energy, transport, agriculture, and infrastructure, adds another dimension to this policy. Moscow’s outreach should, therefore, be understood as an effort to protect its own interests and expand its regional options. Russia’s close ties with Kabul won’t automatically ensure action against anti-Pakistan terrorists. Second, Russia’s recognition of the Taliban has important implications for Pakistan’s diplomatic leverage. For years, Islamabad’s geographical proximity, economic connections, and historical links with the Taliban gave it considerable access to Kabul. Russian recognition gives Kabul an additional source of international legitimacy. Its expanding relations with Moscow also offer the Taliban another channel for diplomatic engagement, security cooperation, and economic opportunity. The more external partners Kabul acquires, the less dependent it may feel on Islamabad for diplomatic access and international engagement. This does not mean that Pakistan’s influence will disappear. Geography, cross-border commerce, people-to-people links, and the management of shared security concerns remain important. However, these factors do not automatically translate into political compliance. Pakistan’s leverage will increasingly depend on whether it can demonstrate the mutual benefits of cooperation rather than rely on historical relationships or geographical realities alone. Third, Russia’s approach to the TTP will be the most consequential test. Islamabad’s central security concern is that terrorist groups operating from Afghan territory threaten Pakistan’s citizens and security personnel. The Taliban authorities’ generalised statement is that Afghan territory will not be used against other countries, but they are reluctant to specifically say that Afghan territory will not be allowed to be used against Pakistan. Moscow’s priorities, however, do not match Pakistan’s. Russia’s immediate security concerns centre particularly on IS-K and the threat of extremist violence spreading into Central Asia and Russia itself. Although the Taliban also oppose IS-K, this convergence does not necessarily mean Moscow will place Pakistan’s concerns about the TTP at the centre of its Afghan policy. Pakistan should, therefore, avoid assuming that Russia’s close relations with Kabul will automatically produce action against anti-Pakistan terrorists. Russian influence could provide an additional diplomatic channel, but its effectiveness will depend on Moscow’s willingness to address the TTP issue and the Taliban leadership’s readiness to respond. Fourth, Russia’s interest in regional stability gives it a potential role in facilitating dialogue, reducing tensions and encouraging practical cooperation. Pakistan should welcome constructive Russian involvement without outsourcing its Afghan policy to Moscow. The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation could provide a useful multilateral framework. Pakistan, Russia, China, and the Central Asian states share an interest in preventing Afghanistan from becoming a base for transnational terrorism. Coordinated intelligence exchanges, border-security cooperation, counter-narcotics measures, and structured consultations with Kabul could help establish a regional approach. Such cooperation would be more sustainable than expecting any single country to exercise decisive influence over the Taliban. Fifth, Pakistan needs to adapt its Afghan policy to a more competitive diplomatic environment. Islamabad should deepen engagement with Russia while maintaining direct communication with the Taliban leadership. It should also coordinate with China, the Central Asian republics, and other relevant regional actors to develop a common understanding of the threats emanating from Afghanistan. At the bilateral level, Pakistan has to involve the Taliban in a meaningful dialogue and create a workable environment that builds the Taliban regime’s stake in the mutual benefits of the two countries. This could include arrangements to exchange information on terrorist networks, investigate cross-border incidents, prevent attacks, and maintain communication between security officials. Economic cooperation and the facilitation of legitimate trade should accompany these measures, giving both sides practical incentives to reduce tensions. Diplomatically, Russia’s Afghan outreach is thus neither an inevitable strategic setback for Pakistan nor a guarantee of improved regional security. It is a development that reflects the Taliban’s efforts to widen their international options and Moscow’s decision to protect its own interests. Whether this produces greater stability or further competition will depend on how regional states use their expanding diplomatic channels. Pakistan will have to carefully observe that Russia’s engagement helps address the region’s shared security concerns. Islamabad’s influence over Kabul will ultimately depend less on who has the closest relationship with the Taliban and more on who can help produce practical results: a secure border, action against militant violence, functioning trade routes and a stable regional environment. The writer is a former special representative of Pakistan for Afghanistan. He served as Pakistan’s ambassador to the UAE and Iran.
articles.author: Asif Durrani

articles.title: A huddle in Tehran
articles.content: LAST month, Iarguedin this space that Iran is emerging as a big regional power to our west. The question I left hanging was whether it would use its newfound centrality to avenge the past or to build a future. Last week offered the first real glimpse of an answer. On Oct 26, Saudi Arabia’s defence minister, Pakistan’s defence chief, and Turkiye’s intelligence chiefsat down in Tehranwith Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council. The joint statement that followed was thin, pledging only continued dialogue on regional peace and security. But the significance of the Tehran huddle lies less in what was said than in the fact that it happened at all, and where. Consider who came. The three visitors are the signatories of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, signed in August, a pact many read as a hedge against precisely the kind of Iran I described last month. Saudi Arabia was struck repeatedly by Iran during the war, hosted American forces that attacked Iran, and isunder fire from the Houthiseven now. Yet, the Saudi defence minister led the delegation, and they travelled to Tehran. Not Riyadh, Ankara or Islamabad, nor a neutral venue like Doha or Muscat. When three of the region’s largest military powers, one of them nuclear-armed, come to your capital to talk about regional security, they are acknowledging that no regional security arrangement is possible without you, and that the road to one runs through your door. For a country that spent four decades behind a wall of sanctions and was treated as a problem to be contained rather than a party to be consulted, this is a milestone. The significance of the Tehran huddle lies less in what was said than in the fact that it happened at all, and where. It also happened in the teeth of American pressure. Washington was openly weighing a fresh round of strikes, US forces were reportedly ready to move within 96 hours of an order, and a naval blockade was choking Iran’s southern ports. The region’s middle powers came anyway, having concluded that Iran would still be standing after this war and that they need a working relationship with it whatever Washington decided. The second thing worth noticing is what Iran chose to emphasise. Rezaei told state television that Tehran and its three guests had agreed that the region’s security is to be achieved through the countries of the region. A senior Pakistani security official told Reuters the meeting’s primary aim was a regional mechanism to prevent military attacks between them. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said for months that Tehran will welcome any regional security arrangement that excludes foreign forces. Put these together and the outline of the order Iran wants comes into view. It rests on three pillars: non-aggression among the states of the region, an alignment of their interests, and the exit of outside powers, above all America, from the business of guaranteeing Gulf security. This is a window into the kind of power Iran wants to project. Last month, I worried that once the Americans were gone, the Iranian military machine would turn its gaze to the riches of the Gulf monarchs and present bill after bill. That risk has not gone away. But the posture on display in Tehran was not that of a power seeking to dominate its neighbours by force. It was that of a power seeking to become the indispensable centre of a regional system it helps design. The China analogy is instructive here too. In 1954, with Beijing still shunned by much of the world, Zhou Enlai put forward the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence in negotiations with India. Mutual non-aggression sat at their heart, alongside non-interference in internal affairs. Non-aggression is the language of a power confident of its own weight, which wants its neighbours to accommodate it rather than fear it. There is hard strategic logic beneath the soft language. A non-aggression architecture without foreign forces is the one in which Iran’s advantages count most. Take American bases and carriers out of the Gulf, and Iran’s hold over Hormuz, its missile arsenal, and its network of allies make it the pre-eminent power on the Gulf littoral by default. In that setting, a non-aggression pact is not a concession but a way of having one’s pre-eminence ratified by one’s neighbours. Nor did the idea originate in Tehran. In May, Saudi Arabia itself floated a non-aggression pact between Iran and the states of the region, reportedly modelled on the 1975 Helsinki Accords. Iran is now taking an idea its rivals put on the table and making it the organising principle of an order with itself at the centre. That, too, is what emerging powers do. None of this is settled. The factional contest I described last month is playing out in plain sight. The hard-line daily Kayhan treated oil above $115 a barrel as proof that pressure on shipping works better than diplomacy, while moderate papers warn of a wave of bankruptcies in Isfahan, Tabriz, and Arak as the blockade bites. Which camp prevails will decide whether the language of non-aggression is here to stay. Pakistan has a particular stake in all this. An Iran that seeks pre-eminence through a regional architecture is a neighbour Pakistan can work with, and help shape from the inside. An Iran that seeks it through reparations, tolls, and coercion would place us in an impossible position between our western neighbour and the Gulf states on which so much of our economy depends. The huddle does not answer last month’s question. But it shows that the option of building a future is on the table, in Iran’s own words, and that its neighbours are prepared to engage on those terms. That is a milestone. Whether it becomes a trajectory depends on whether the voices in Tehran speaking the language of non-aggression win the argument at home, and whether Washington, after its elections on Nov 3, lets them. The writer is a business and economy journalist.
articles.author: Khurram Husain

articles.title: From such seeds
articles.content: ON Nov 3 this year, Aitchison College, Lahore, will celebrate its 140th birthday. It has outlived the former Indian Civil Service which lasted 87 years (1858-1947), and is almost twice the age of the ICS’ successor, the Pakistan Civil Service. In many ways, the path and purpose of Aitchison College have run parallel to both, in that it has produced generations of pre- and post-independence leadership. At the time of independence, in August 1947, there were 980 ICS officers. They comprised 468 British and 512 Indian locals. Of the latter, 352 were Hindus and 101 Muslims. The remainder were a smattering of other faiths. The first Indian to be admitted to the ICS was Satyendranath Tagore, in 1863. Until the 1950s, the ICS remained a misogynist preserve, as Aitchison College is even today. The first woman to be admitted into the Indian Administrative Service (IAS) was Anna Rajam Malhotra, who joined its 1951 batch. Initially, the Union Public Service Commission Board after her viva voce interview tried to discourage her from joining the IAS. It offered her the Foreign Service and Central Services, because these were ‘more suitable for women’. She resisted their blandishments, and in time rose in her career to become India’s first secretary. Between 1950 and 2020, out of 11,569 officers who entered the IAS, only 1,527 (roughly 13 per cent) were women. The gender imbalance has been corrected since. The 2024 batch contained 41pc women. That is lower than the counterpart representation in Pakistan’s civil service where, out of 217 fresh entrants into the 54th Common Training Programme (2026), 117 were men and almost half (100) women. Some of them will rise (male prejudice notwithstanding) to become secretaries in the federal government, as once the brave and unsung Miss Gulzar Bano had done. In November 1947, Miss Gulzar Bano and her nine younger siblings travelled without their parents from Lucknow to Lahore. All she carried with her was a slip of paper containing the address of a relative living in Model Town. She studied with diligence, often attending school on alternate days as she and her sister had to share the same pair of shoes. In 1950, she sat for the CSS examination, topping the list of successful candidates. After the viva voce, however, the selection board relegated her to the second position because “it lacked confidence in women’s talents”. She suffered a second humiliation when she discovered that she could not join the ‘serious’ services — the CSP, Foreign Service, or the Police. She had to join the Audit and Accounts Service. She reported to the accountant general (Post and Telegraph), who arranged for her desk to be placed in the public hall near the superintendent (her junior). The office had no toilet for ladies. On occasions, she was forced “to take a tonga to Government College” to relieve herself. She reached the top of the bureaucracy’s greasy pole when she became cabinet secretary for a brief period, from June 4 to Dec 14, 1978. She described her 30-year career as a “kind of loneliness which only a single Pakistani woman starting work in the 1950s” could understand. Ms Bano would have been gratified to learn that her example has inspired many women. Ms Tehmina Janjua, for one. In February 2017, she became our first female foreign secretary. Such gender calibration suggests there is hope, were it not for the dismal results of the civil service exams. The results of the CSS 2026 written exam provide grim reading. Out of 17,351 candidates who appeared, only 476 candidates qualified, with a pass rate of 2.7pc. (Incidentally, 239 were men and 237 women.) For details of their results, one is referred by the Federal Public Service Commission to its results portal. Access it, and you will get this message: “No active information available in this section.”The FPSC has itself become a role model of institutionalised inertia. Aspirants to our civil service undoubtedly study hard, pore over articles, digest numerous books, and plough through exam guides. But obviously, that is not enough. They may read everything, yet they learn nothing. Had they been Chinese, they would have had to memorise between 50,000 to 100,000 characters. As it is, some of our senior civil servants, aspiring to be promoted to the level of federal secretaries, have found difficulty in mastering even 26 letters in the English alphabet. Some still think the title of the founder of our nation is ‘Quad-e-Azam’ or ‘Quid-e-Azam’. One is reminded of the senior student at Aitchison College who concluded his recitation of a story once with the innovative word: ‘Theend’.
articles.author: F.S. Aijazuddin

articles.title: Elusive quality
articles.content: EACH year, the noise grows louder and the naming and shaming of public entities reaches its crescendo around budget time. The music sheet remains unchanged, the chorus: ‘cuts in development allocations in the social sectors’. ‘Cacophony’ is a better descriptor. However, what adds insult to injury is that, in keeping with tradition, the health and education ministries have failed to fully utilise even the minuscule allocations they received in the outgoing fiscal year, prompting the Planning Commission to admonish them and donors to protest yet another set of rollover requests from the relevant departments. The development fraternity continues to lament that whatever little is allocated to human development mostly falls under the non-development or recurrent category, and very little, if anything, is left for ‘development’. While successive governments have not overcome the fiscal constraints, real or imagined, in increasing budget allocations to the social sector, the public discourse has also not risen beyond hackneyed criticism. Isn’t it time to ask, recurrent as they may be, why salaries in the education department are considered beyond the pale of development? Yes, the proportion of administrative versus teaching cadres must be debated, but the debate should also expand to include questions such as, ‘what about monitoring and evaluation?’, ‘what about coaching support for teachers?’, ‘what about assessment systems for students and teachers?’ True, AI will play a role, but trained, motivated human resources can’t be ignored. Salaries and career trajectories that attract the country’s best talent must be considered as much a part of development as curricula, textbook content and design, learning aids, and training. The less said about civil works the better. Infrastructure is essential to ensure a safe, conducive learning environment, but boundary walls and rooms alone won’t foster learning outcomes, critical thinking, and problem-solving abilities among students. Education quality can’t improve without quality expenditure. Education quality can’t improve without quality expenditure. No rocket science; it’s just another way of saying ‘bang for the buck’ or stretching the rupee. A low-fee private school in a small building with little to no space for physical training or sports still enjoys more parental trust than a large public school next door with some, if not all, facilities, even though it pays a fraction of the salary a public-sector teacher earns and provides almost no training. While one cannot regulate private schools beyond preventing exploitation, public school teachers can surely be supported to produce better learning outcomes for students. In the next phase, non-performers should be removed. While discussing the quality of expenditure, when was the last time we heard of an independent audit of teacher recruitment, training, and coaching mechanisms in the public sector? What incentives are in place for those who perform well, and what disincentives can be implemented under the current lifelong job guarantee, which is assumed not only by teachers but also the judicial system? Try denying an erring teacher a promotion they believe their years of service warrant, or firing an egregious one, and the courts will issue a stay order and then revoke any proposed disciplinary action, with full payment of arrears accrued during the litigation. We can create as many islands of excellence in this sea of inequity as we like, but we can’t address what ails our education until we adopt a systemic, holistic, and transformative approach to reform. This calls for collective leadership, with the choir led by the very children whose futures are at stake, and with the voices of their parents and communities heard. People change systems. People must exercise their agency and stop voting for transfers and postings, or for petty dispute resolution at the revenue department or police station level. They must demand that party manifestos specifically address issues with far-reaching impact on future generations, and then hold their representatives, whether in the ruling alliance or in opposition, accountable. Responsive governance and politics require compromise; only a collective of citizens can ensure that these trade-offs benefit future generations rather than private gain. While the enigma of what truly guarantees national sovereignty is unresolved, the demand for increased human development allocations must be paired with insistence on expenditure quality to ensure development effectiveness. A matriculate able to read, comprehend, and calculate at a level commensurate with 10 years of schooling is not too much to ask. If this cannot be achieved, budgets, whether recurrent or developmental, yield nothing but deficits. The writer is a poet. His latest publication is a collection of satire essays titled Rindana.
articles.author: Shahzad Sharjeel

articles.title: Restructuring plans
articles.content: THE PPP appears quite perturbed over the fact that the creation of new provinces or administrative units continues to be discussed. Speaking at an event in Karachi on Tuesday, PPP chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardariassertedthat no one outside Sindh could decide its future. “So we should now put a full stop to this conversation as well.” The Bhutto scion said the people of Sindh and their elected representatives had “given their verdict” on this matter, ostensibly referring to a Sindh Assemblyresolutionin early September. Solely on principle, his position cannot be faulted. The Constitution does lay out a clear process for decisions of this sort, and it gives the elected assembly of each affected province a final say on the matter. Of course, there are public representatives from the same province, albeit from other parties, who disagree with the PPP chairperson’s view. However, that disagreement alone cannot be used to override a defined legal process. Unfortunately, as recent events in KP have shown, the public’s mandate and verdicts delivered through the ballot box can be brushed aside if the centre is sufficiently motivated. For KP, its decisions are now being made not by its elected representatives, but byadministratorshandpicked by Islamabad. It can be argued that this is, perhaps, not a fair comparison, but Mr Bhutto-Zardari should still realise that his position may not hold as much force as he thinks it does, and it will, therefore, not be as easy to bury this agenda as he would like. There are many voices within the federal government’s ruling coalition that are actively advocating for the division of all provinces into more ‘manageable’ units. As was seen in KP, such voices can be amplified to find causa proxima, the trigger for an intervention, if it comes to that. Therefore, a better course of action would be to address governance grievances proactively. The primary reason for governance failure in Pakistan is not the geographical size of the existing provinces but the reluctance of provincial capitals to empower local bodies. Few can convincingly argue that the local government system, as it exists today, is capable of positive change at the grassroots level. At the same time, simply creating more provinces will only add heavy, expensive layers of provincial bureaucracy at a time when Pakistan can ill afford them. There are also steep social costs to consider, as pushing forward without public validation could trigger ethnic strife. Therefore, empowered local bodies remain the best answer to all those issues which seem to warrant a fracturing of the provinces in the eyes of those demanding an administrative restructuring. The decrepit LG system needs to be revitalised, with resources invested in it judiciously. Doing so can improve service delivery at the neighbourhood level in a meaningful way.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Polluted priorities
articles.content: LAHORE is choking again, and the government’s answer is to send more machines onto its streets. On Wednesday, its air quality index reached 296, putting children, outdoor workers, and the elderly at particular risk. Yet Punjab plans to acquire 30 more truck-mounted fog cannons. These can suppress road dust locally, but their ability to reduce the fine particles most harmful to health remains questionable. Authorities must explain what the existing fleet has achieved in terms of measurable pollution reduction before spending more public money. Last year, disruptions to Punjab’s air monitoring network raised suspicions that pollution levels were being hidden; officials cited technical faults. Whether equipment is recording pollution or spraying water, public confidence depends on transparent data and independent scrutiny. A temporary improvement at a pollution hotspot, or near a monitoring station, cannot prove that the city’s air is becoming safer. Monitoring should expose pollution. Punjab must publish continuous readings and independent assessments of its interventions. It should also fund research into the relative contributions of traffic, industry, construction, and crop burning, how these change with the seasons, and which measures actually reduce exposure. That scientific effort must extend beyond the border. Punjab officials say easterly winds have been bringing polluted air from India into Lahore. But this does not absolve Pakistan of responsibility for its own emissions. The air over the two Punjabs is shared, and both populations suffer when political hostility obstructs cooperation. Calls for joint action are not new. Cooperation was proposed with Indian Punjab in 2017 and 2024. Yet neither initiative led to sustained cooperation. Environmental diplomacy with New Delhi should be prioritised, despite wider tensions. Both sides could begin by exchanging verified air-quality and weather data, jointly studying the movement of pollutants and developing common approaches to agricultural burning and industrial emissions. Universities and scientific institutions could help build a shared evidence base. At home, dedicated research funding, stronger monitoring, and open evaluation of anti-smog spending are essential. Enforcement must continue, but decisions should follow evidence, not the visibility of machinery on city roads. Until the air itself improves, no amount of official activity can be called progress.
articles.author: Editorial
